2026-07-24 · ♲

Everyone knows AI is sycophantic at this point, but the ways it manifests keep surprising me. AI will never say no to you, even if what you ask it to do is incoherent. Even if there’s no sense in it at all.

The other day I spoke at length with someone who claimed to be building something profound—some kind of knowledge network that they struggled to articulate when pressed and eventually told me “I just needed to see it.”

The prompt history was borderline schizophrenic nonsense. It read like a conspiracy theorist rattling off a series of disparate patterns and asking the system to fill in the gaps between them. There was no real world context and no practical application. But unable to say no, it started building, and the result was an enormous network of vector concepts that, despite their utter meaninglessness, “fit” together in a coherent, runnable system. It was essentially a massive “hello world” application, but with so much code that the author believed they had created something extraordinary.

2026-02-01 · ♴

Stuck culture gets a lot of talk these days. Here’s my theory on why it’s happening:

Culture evolves at the margins. Nobody pulls something genuinely new out of a vacuum. Ideas morph slowly over time, sometimes intentionally, but more often by accident. When people set out to do one thing—make music of a certain genre, design a house, shoot a film—tiny variations in the tools used and the people involved and the habits of consumers and audiences used to have unpredictable outcomes that were occasionally loved and celebrated. Once upon a time, subpar Russian manufacturing technique lead to the creation of a camera whose images were distorted with a blue-green hue. The images were initially labeled poor quality, but eventually they picked up a following of people who actually liked the look. Eventually it became so popular that some app developers created an app to mimic the look on digital photos via “filters”. That app is Instagram.

That Russian camera existed in the margins. It didn’t excel at anything that anyone would have thought to optimize for. Instead, it created new culture. It made a new category for itself altogether. A category which today is specifically sought out and optimized for.

The is no limit to these undiscovered categories. At least not in theory. But increasingly, we live in a world that makes them impossible to discover. This is because the quantified, digitized, mechanized world has no margins.

When we build houses with Home Depot parts and plant lawns with Home Depot grass and grow food with Monsanto seed and buy food from grocery stores where every item needs to be labeled and registered and have a scannable SKU and make music with digital instruments with a finite number of preprogrammed sounds and buy products that all come from the same factories, there is no possibility for the kinds of human scale variation that creates new culture. A man who sets out to build a guitar may make a random choice, or a mistake, or introduce a feature which eventually leads to the creation of an entirely new use for the instrument. But the guy who buys a Stratocaster from Guitar Center has an all but predetermined destiny.

Systemification, the thing has been calling the machine, blocks the evolution of culture. That’s why we’re stuck.

2025-10-13 · ♲

There is religion, which is spiritual, and there is religious thinking, which is a style of thinking meant for talking about spirituality, but which has bled through to secular conversation and is wreaking havoc on our ability to think clearly.

Definition

If you dedicate yourself to a cause but cannot give a definite answer to the question, “How much is enough?”, you are guilty of religious thinking.

Examples

In spiritual religion, this typically manifests as follows:

Q: How much good do I need to do in order to not be a sinner? A: You should do as much good as possible, but no matter how much good you do, you will always be a sinner.

Q: How much do I need to meditate to become enlightened? A: You should seek enlightenment in every aspect of your life, but you can never fully achieve enlightenment.

In secular discussion, it looks more like this:

Q: How much do we need to cut taxes? A: You should always cut taxes, and no matter how much you cut them, it will never be enough.

Q: How many government services should we provide? A: All government services are inherently inadequate and should be better funded and more comprehensive.

Q: How much “healing/learning/atoning” do we need to do before we can move past [historical tragedy]? A: You should factor atonement for [historical tragedy] into everything you do, but no matter how much you do, you can never actually be healed, and the debt can never be repaid.

Religious thinking detaches you from the concrete facts that are required to make fruitful decisions. If you cannot measure your progress toward an achievable goal, all you’re doing is wasting time and money.

2025-08-04 · ♼

There’s a distinct archetype in housing now that I’ve been calling the “Boomer Special”

It’s a house that has been both upgraded and neglected simultaneously. Or rather: the upgrades contribute to the neglect.

In a boomer special, the marked up original floors have been replaced with LVP, but not throughout the home, and never more than one room at a time, and each phase used a slightly different style of flooring, and the transitions between them are either marked by a plastic transition strip or left as an unfinished gap to be completed “when I get around to it.”

In a boomer special, every appliance has been modified with a plastic dollar store contraption. The toilets all have broken pneumatic buttons that were in theory supposed to save water, but being dollar store quality, they broke within a week and now everyone has to use the high flush option every time. Net result: no water savings, and a hole in the side of the toilet where the proper handle used to be.

In a boomer special, things that can be maintained are deemed “old” and are instead thrown out and replaced with plastic simulacra that cannot be maintained, and whose lifespan is a fraction of the original’s. All appliances have been replaced with touch button devices from Alibaba that are broken even when they’re working

In a boomer special, nothing is usable for its original purpose. The garage was converted to a bedroom. The fireplaces have fake logs and can’t burn wood. The backyard is has been stripped of all natural elements because:

In a boomer special, low maintenance is the only priority, so anything that requires effort has been removed, regardless of how rewarding it is. No plants, no gardens, no natural materials that require sanding or polishing.

And finally, in a boomer special, all these things are seen as “improvements”, and they expect you to pay a premium for them.

2025-05-30 · ♹

I watched Jordan Peterson’s Jubilee debate last night and in the middle of it I figured it all out. I know exactly why he’s controversial. It has nothing to do with him being right or wrong.

Most people are highly reductive in their pursuit of knowledge, and they think definitions are absolute. Almost everyone in this debate started out by trying to get Peterson to define something so that they could point out scenarios in which the definition falls short, and when they do that, they think they've discredited his him. When instead of conceding, Peterson then proceeds to make his definition more robust, they roll their eyes and say that he's just leaning on vague definitions in order to make it impossible for him to be wrong. But that's not at all what's happening.

What's really happening is that Peterson understands intuitively that there are no absolutes--that language is imperfect and that everything can only be described imperfectly. When he dodges being called a Christian, it's not because he's afraid of the implications, it's because he can see that the person calling him a Christian has their own concept of what that means, and that saying, "Yes" to a naive person will be read as an absolute (you are a Christian, therefor...) when it fact it's a relative. I thought his analogy about literature later in the debate was extremely apt: Someone asked him "if Christianity is a spectrum, what percentage Christian do I need to be in order to be considered Christian", and Peterson responded, if literature is a spectrum, and we agree that a porno mag is on one end and Dostoevsky is on the other, what is the cutoff for a piece of writing to be considered great? The idea being that though there is no answer to that question, that in no way undermines the idea that there is nevertheless a distinct category called Great Literature. That we can debate what falls into that category in no way suggests that the category doesn't exist.

This is the way Peterson thinks about the world: He recognizes that though absolutes do exist, they are impossible to define with language. But that does not mean that they cannot be understood or aren't worth pursuing. What it means is that one must approach them with the understanding that definitions themselves are fluid, just like the category of great literature is fluid, and are only useful insofar as they help us to learn about and understand the absolutes intuitively.

Ultimately I think this is a bottom-up vs top-down approach to the world. Do definitions create things, or do things create definitions? What is a cloud, for example? Can you define it? Are 3 water molecules in the air a cloud? Or do there need to be more? If more, how many more? Does it need to be visible? How close together do they need to be? How long to they need to be together for? What if there are only two water molecules and one bit of carbon trapped between them? Yes, we have a discrete definition for a cloud, but that does not mean something that falls outside that definition might not also be a cloud. Something is not either a cloud or not a cloud. Rather, a cloud is a pattern. Things can be more or less cloudlike. Everything that exists is some percentage cloud.

The reductionists in this debate would ask, "Oh, so your definition of a cloud is that everyone is a cloud? Am I a cloud?" thinking that this statement sounds ridiculous and therefor disproves the whole concept. But in fact it’s true, and all it really proves is their lack of understanding of the relative world we live in.
